Selected recommendations:

•   National or sectoral framework: Establish a technology-neutral cybersecurity framework
    applicable to critical ports that defines cybersecurity obligations, covering governance, risk

question: In A Global Port Resilience Gap, compare incident-reporting percentages for high-income versus low- and middle-income ports and calculate the gap.
answer: High-income ports report incidents to a response team at an 83% rate, while low- and middle-income ports report at a 56% rate. The gap is 27 percentage points.

results.text: The World Bank survey highlights disparities in cybersecurity practices between high-income and low- & middle-income ports. Key findings include that 83% of high-income ports report incidents to a response team, compared to 56% of low- & middle-income ports. Additionally, 79% of high-income ports have conducted cybersecurity risk assessments in the past 24 months, while only 56% of low- & middle-income ports have done so. Furthermore, 84% of high-income ports provide regular cybersecurity training, in contrast to 49% of low- & middle-income ports.

A Global Port Resilience Gap
                  A Tale of Two Ports

    The World Bank survey received 109 responses from ports, port authorities, and maritime
  organizations worldwide. Respondents were distributed across the World Bank income groups
      as follows: 48 from high-income countries (44 percent), 23 from upper-middle-income
     countries (21 percent), 30 from lower-middle-income countries (28 percent), and 8 from
 low-income countries (7 percent). The results reveal important disparities between high-income
 and low- and middle-income countries in their ability to address cyber risks. Yet across all income
                      groups, no port ecosystem appears fully cyber-proof.

The World Bank survey shows that recent risk assessments are far more common among
respondents from ports in high-income countries than among ports in low- and middle-income
countries (Figure 7). Among port stakeholders in high-income countries, 79 percent reported having
conducted such an assessment in the past 24 months. In upper-middle-income (61 percent) and
lower-middle-income (57 percent) contexts, this share is much lower. It drops to 38 percent among
respondents from ports in low-income countries. This is likely due to the higher maturity levels of the
legal requirements in high-income countries, as illustrated by the examples listed in Table 1 in the
previous chapter.
